df61824d-5b86-429e-852e-a412b76cf40b: My approach is to turn agent behavior into testable claims before any production deployment. I start by mapping the workflow, expected outputs, likely failure modes, and acceptance criteria tied to the business task—accuracy, reliability, and end-user usefulness, which connects directly to Arizent’s need to continuously test agents over time. For LLM and agent work, I would build a fixed evaluation set with edge cases, run repeated tests across prompts or seeds, inspect intermediate reasoning/tool steps, and require evidence traces rather than judging only the final answer. In my botanical reasoning prototype, I used constrained iterative planning, per-step information-gain evaluation, and knowledge-graph evidence aggregation. I also use controlled evaluations and sham/randomized controls to catch leakage, unstable behavior, or misleading causal claims before release, then document limitations clearly for stakeholders.
41dc2274-74f3-47e7-8b4c-6e4966c159db: The most complex agentic workflow I built was a multi-agent botanical reasoning prototype at Arborphy AI for applied plant identification. The problem was that visual plant ID can mix species identity, organ morphology, and photographic-scale artifacts, so the workflow needed to gather evidence rather than rely on one model output. I built specialized visual-analysis agents, autonomous tool generation, constrained iterative planning, per-step information-gain evaluation, and knowledge-graph-based evidence aggregation. I also connected this work to controlled experiments around BioCLIP, DINOv3, and EfficientNet representations, using reproducible research pipelines and interactive analysis tools. My specific contribution was the end-to-end design and implementation of the prototype and the surrounding evaluation workflow, which is close to Arizent’s need for tested, reliable agents tied to real data workflows.
b62e4715-9490-4eb8-87ce-090a430d1a12: A good example is from my Columbia Zuckerman Institute research assistant work on two-photon calcium-imaging denoising. I found that one result did not line up numerically when comparing spatial-component behavior with reconstructed-video outputs, which mattered because downstream analysis depended on trusting the preprocessing. I diagnosed the issue by analyzing denoising at both the spatial-component and reconstructed-video levels and tracing the discrepancy to PMD’s blockwise spatial update. I then implemented a fixed-temporal-basis least-squares refitting correction and contributed it through pull requests. The outcome was a corrected, more reproducible research pipeline, which I also helped turn into a downloadable software package with public documentation and step-by-step guides for wet-lab researchers.
